title: Chemical Bonding

notes.heading: 1. Ionic Lattice, Fajans' Polarizability Rules & VSEPR Hybridization
notes.proseLatex: Ionic bonding is favoured by low ionization enthalpy, high electron gain affinity, and large lattice energy ($\propto \frac{q^+ q^-}{r^+ + r^-}$). By Fajans' rules, a small highly-charged cation + large polarizable anion increases covalent character ($\text{LiCl} > \text{NaCl} > \text{KCl}$; $\text{AlCl}_3 > \text{MgCl}_2 > \text{NaCl}$). Steric number $\text{SN} = \frac{1}{2}(V + M - C + A)$ gives hybridization: $2\to sp$ (linear $180^\circ$), $3\to sp^2$ (trigonal planar $120^\circ$), $4\to sp^3$ ($\text{CH}_4\;109.5^\circ > \text{NH}_3\;107^\circ > \text{H}_2\text{O}\;104.5^\circ$ as $\text{LP--LP} > \text{LP--BP} > \text{BP--BP}$), $5\to sp^3d$, $6\to sp^3d^2$.

keyFormulas.label: Steric Number Hybridization Formula
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Predict hybridization and molecular shape of SF4, XeF2,XeF4, I3-, ClF3.

examples.problemLatex: Find the hybridization, lone pairs on Xe, and molecular shape of $\text{XeF}_4$.
stepsLatex: With $4$ bond pairs and $6 - 4 = 2$ trans lone pairs, molecular shape is square planar (dipole moment $\mu = 0$).

notes.heading: 2. Molecular Orbital Theory (MOT), Bond Order & O₂ Paramagnetism
notes.proseLatex: For homonuclear diatomics ($Z_{\text{total}} \le 14$: $\text{B}_2, \text{C}_2, \text{N}_2$), $\pi_{2p}$ lies below $\sigma_{2p_z}$; for $Z_{\text{total}} > 14$ ($\text{O}_2, \text{F}_2$), $\sigma_{2p_z}$ lies below $\pi_{2p}$. Bond order is $\text{BO} = \frac{1}{2}(N_b - N_a)$: higher $\text{BO}$ means shorter bond length and higher bond dissociation energy ($\text{BO}=0$ means molecule does not exist, e.g. $\text{He}_2$). Critically, MOT explains that $\text{O}_2$ ($\text{BO}=2$) and $\text{B}_2$ ($\text{BO}=1$) are PARAMAGNETIC due to two unpaired $\pi^*$ / $\pi$ electrons!

keyFormulas.label: MOT Bond Order & O₂ Series Ordering
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Rank bond order, bond length, and paramagnetism of diatomic species.

notes.heading: 3. Dipole Moment & Intermolecular vs Intramolecular Hydrogen Bonding
notes.proseLatex: Vector dipole moment $\vec{\mu} = q\vec{d}$ ($1\text{ D} = 3.336\times 10^{-30}\text{ C\,m}$) cancels to ZERO in symmetric geometries ($\text{CO}_2, \text{BF}_3, \text{CCl}_4, \text{XeF}_4, \text{XeF}_2$). Notice $\mu(\text{NH}_3) > \mu(\text{NF}_3)$ because the lone-pair dipole adds to $\text{N--H}$ bond dipoles in $\text{NH}_3$ but opposes $\text{N--F}$ bond dipoles in $\text{NF}_3$! Intermolecular H-bonding ($\text{H--F, H--O, H--N}$) raises boiling point ($\text{H}_2\text{O} \gg \text{H}_2\text{S}$), whereas intramolecular H-bonding in *o*-nitrophenol makes it MORE steam-volatile than *p*-nitrophenol.

keyFormulas.label: Dipole Moment & Percent Ionic Character
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Compare NH3 vs NF3 dipoles, cis vs trans isomers, and H-bonding boiling trends.

wbjeebTraps: Classic MOT trap: $\text{O}_2$ ($16\,e^-$) and $\text{B}_2$ ($10\,e^-$) are PARAMAGNETIC despite having an even total number of electrons!
$\mu(\text{NH}_3 = 1.47\text{ D}) > \mu(\text{NF}_3 = 0.24\text{ D})$ even though fluorine is more electronegative than hydrogen.
*o*-Nitrophenol has LOWER boiling point (higher steam volatility) than *p*-nitrophenol due to chelated intramolecular H-bonding.
